It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

The message is `error: usage: cli.js json|keys` when the argument is not exactly one of the two mode words, and otherwise `error: line N: <reason>` where the reason is one of `expected a name`, `expected a value`, `expected key = value`, `expected = in an inline table`, `unterminated string`, `unterminated array`, `unterminated inline table`, `unterminated table header`, `invalid escape \<character>`, `invalid value <text>`, `trailing text after a value`, `trailing text after a table header`, `key <path> is defined twice` with the path counted from the root, `table <path> is defined twice`, `<path> is not a table`, and `<path> is not an array of tables`.

15: /** Require the rest of a line to be blank or a comment. */
16: function endOfLine(reader, what) {
17:   reader.skip()
18:   const rest = reader.peek()
19:   if (rest !== undefined && rest !== '#' && rest !== ';') throw new ConfError(`trailing text after ${what}`)
20: }
21: 
22: /**
23:  * Parse the whole document into a tree of tables, arrays of tables, and values.
24:  * @param lines - the input lines, in order.
25:  * @returns the root table.
26:  * @throws {ConfError} carrying a `line` for any malformed or conflicting directive.
27:  */
28: export function parse(lines) {
29:   const root = table()
30:   let current = root
31:   let currentPath = []
32:   for (let index = 0; index < lines.length; index += 1) {
33:     const raw = lines[index]
34:     try {
35:       const reader = new Reader(raw)
36:       reader.skip()
37:       const first = reader.peek()
38:       if (first === undefined || first === '#' || first === ';') continue
39:       if (first === '[') {
40:         reader.at += 1
41:         const array = reader.eat('[')
42:         const parts = reader.name()
43:         if (!reader.eat(']') || (array && !reader.eat(']'))) throw new ConfError('unterminated table header')
44:         endOfLine(reader, 'a table header')
45:         const parent = descend(root, parts.slice(0, -1), [])
46:         const last = parts[parts.length - 1]
47:         const held = parent.value.get(last)
48:         if (array) {
49:           if (held !== undefined && held.type !== 'tables') throw new ConfError(`${parts.join('.')} is not an array of tables`)
50:           const list = held ?? { type: 'tables', value: [] }
51:           const fresh = table()
52:           fresh.explicit = true
53:           list.value.push(fresh)
54:           parent.value.set(last, list)
55:           current = fresh
56:         } else {
57:           if (held !== undefined && held.type !== 'table') throw new ConfError(`${parts.join('.')} is not a table`)
58:           if (held !== undefined && held.explicit) throw new ConfError(`table ${parts.join('.')} is defined twice`)
59:           const fresh = held ?? table()
60:           fresh.explicit = true
61:           parent.value.set(last, fresh)
62:           current = fresh
63:         }
64:         currentPath = parts
65:         continue
66:       }
67:       const parts = reader.name()
68:       reader.skip()
69:       if (!reader.eat('=')) throw new ConfError('expected key = value')
70:       const held = reader.value([...currentPath, ...parts].join('.'))
71:       endOfLine(reader, 'a value')
72:       const target = descend(current, parts.slice(0, -1), currentPath)
73:       const last = parts[parts.length - 1]
74:       if (target.value.has(last)) throw new ConfError(`key ${[...currentPath, ...parts].join('.')} is defined twice`)
75:       target.value.set(last, held)
76:     } catch (error) {
77:       if (!(error instanceof ConfError)) throw error
78:       error.line = index + 1
79:       throw error
80:     }
81:   }
82:   return root
83: }

85: /** The plain JSON value of one node, with every table's keys sorted. */
86: export function toJson(node) {
87:   if (node.type === 'table') {
88:     return Object.fromEntries([...node.value.keys()].sort().map(key => [key, toJson(node.value.get(key))]))
89:   }
90:   if (node.type === 'tables' || node.type === 'array') return node.value.map(toJson)
91:   return node.value
92: }
93: 
94: /**
95:  * Every node below the root, as a dotted path and the type it holds.
96:  * @param node - the node to walk.
97:  * @param path - the path already walked.
98:  * @returns one `{ path, type }` per node below this one, tables' keys in sorted order.
99:  */
100: export function walk(node, path = '') {
101:   const out = []
102:   if (node.type === 'table') {
103:     for (const key of [...node.value.keys()].sort()) {
104:       const child = node.value.get(key)
105:       const childPath = path === '' ? key : `${path}.${key}`
106:       out.push({ path: childPath, type: child.type === 'tables' ? 'array' : child.type })
107:       out.push(...walk(child, childPath))
108:     }
109:     return out
110:   }
111:   if (node.type === 'tables' || node.type === 'array') {
112:     node.value.forEach((child, index) => {
113:       const childPath = `${path}[${index}]`
114:       out.push({ path: childPath, type: child.type === 'tables' ? 'array' : child.type })
115:       out.push(...walk(child, childPath))
116:     })
117:   }
118:   return out
119: }

3: /** Raised for input the specification rejects; `line` is filled in by the caller. */
4: export class ConfError extends Error {
5:   /**
6:    * @param message - the reported reason.
7:    */
8:   constructor(message) {
9:     super(message)
10:     this.name = 'ConfError'
11:   }
12: }

14: /** A bare name: letters, digits, underscore and dash. */
15: const BARE = /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/u
16: 
17: /** An integer: an optional sign and digit runs joined by single underscores. */
18: const INTEGER = /^[+-]?[0-9]+(?:_[0-9]+)*$/u
19: 
20: /** A float: an integer part, then a fraction, an exponent, or both. */
21: const FLOAT = /^[+-]?[0-9]+(?:_[0-9]+)*(?:\.[0-9]+(?:_[0-9]+)*)?(?:[eE][+-]?[0-9]+(?:_[0-9]+)*)?$/u
22: 
23: /** The escapes a basic string carries. */
24: const ESCAPES = { '"': '"', '\\': '\\', n: '\n', t: '\t', r: '\r', 0: '\0' }
25: 
26: /** Join a path counted from the root with the name of something under it. */
27: function under(path, rest) {
28:   return path === '' ? rest : `${path}.${rest}`
29: }

31: /** A cursor over one line's text, shared by the name reader and the value reader. */
32: export class Reader {
33:   /**
34:    * @param text - the line, or the part of it still to read.
35:    */
36:   constructor(text) {
37:     this.text = text
38:     this.at = 0
39:   }
40: 
41:   /** Skip spaces and tabs. */
42:   skip() {
43:     while (this.text[this.at] === ' ' || this.text[this.at] === '\t') this.at += 1
44:   }
45: 
46:   /** The character at the cursor, or `undefined` past the end. */
47:   peek() {
48:     return this.text[this.at]
49:   }
50: 
51:   /** Consume the given text when it sits at the cursor. */
52:   eat(what) {
53:     if (!this.text.startsWith(what, this.at)) return false
54:     this.at += what.length
55:     return true
56:   }
57: 
58:   /** Read one quoted string, decoding a basic string's escapes. */
59:   string() {
60:     const quote = this.text[this.at]
61:     this.at += 1
62:     let value = ''
63:     for (;;) {
64:       const character = this.text[this.at]
65:       if (character === undefined) throw new ConfError('unterminated string')
66:       if (character === quote) {
67:         this.at += 1
68:         return value
69:       }
70:       if (quote === "'" || character !== '\\') {
71:         value += character
72:         this.at += 1
73:         continue
74:       }
75:       const marker = this.text[this.at + 1]
76:       if (marker !== undefined && marker in ESCAPES) {
77:         value += ESCAPES[marker]
78:         this.at += 2
79:         continue
80:       }
81:       if (marker === 'u' && /^[0-9A-Fa-f]{4}/u.test(this.text.slice(this.at + 2))) {
82:         value += String.fromCharCode(Number.parseInt(this.text.slice(this.at + 2, this.at + 6), 16))
83:         this.at += 6
84:         continue
85:       }
86:       throw new ConfError(`invalid escape \\${marker ?? ''}`)
87:     }
88:   }
89: 
90:   /**
91:    * Read one dotted name, whose parts are bare words or basic strings.
92:    * @returns the parts, in order.
93:    * @throws {ConfError} when a part is missing or malformed.
94:    */
95:   name() {
96:     const parts = []
97:     for (;;) {
98:       this.skip()
99:       const character = this.peek()
100:       if (character === '"' || character === "'") parts.push(this.string())

102:         const start = this.at
103:         while (this.peek() !== undefined && BARE.test(this.peek())) this.at += 1
104:         const word = this.text.slice(start, this.at)
105:         if (word === '') throw new ConfError('expected a name')
106:         parts.push(word)
107:       }
108:       this.skip()
109:       if (!this.eat('.')) return parts
110:     }
111:   }
112: 
113:   /**
114:    * Read one value: a scalar, an array, or an inline table.
115:    * @param path - this value's own path counted from the root, so an inline table names its keys in full.
116:    * @returns the value as `{ type, value }`, with `table` and `array` carrying their contents.
117:    * @throws {ConfError} when the value is malformed, or when no value is written where one is required.
118:    */
119:   value(path) {
120:     this.skip()
121:     const character = this.peek()
122:     if (character === undefined) throw new ConfError('expected a value')
123:     if (character === '"' || character === "'") return { type: 'string', value: this.string() }
124:     if (character === '[') return this.array(path)
125:     if (character === '{') return this.inline(path)
126:     const start = this.at
127:     while (this.peek() !== undefined && !' \t,]}'.includes(this.peek())) this.at += 1
128:     const word = this.text.slice(start, this.at)
129:     if (word === '') throw new ConfError('expected a value')
130:     if (word === 'true' || word === 'false') return { type: 'boolean', value: word === 'true' }
131:     const plain = word.replaceAll('_', '')
132:     if (INTEGER.test(word)) return { type: 'integer', value: Number(plain) }
133:     if (FLOAT.test(word)) return { type: 'float', value: Number(plain) }
134:     throw new ConfError(`invalid value ${word}`)
135:   }

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. Walking through an array of tables uses its last element. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the closing bracket is an error.

Every other line is `<dotted name> = <value>`, assigning inside the current table, creating the tables the dots walk through. A name already holding anything may not be assigned again, and a dot may not walk through a name that holds something other than a table or an array of tables.

A value is one of: `true` or `false`; an integer, an optional `+` or `-` and runs of digits joined by single `_`; a float, an integer with a fraction of `.` and digit runs, an exponent of `e` or `E`, an optional sign and digit runs, or both; a basic string in double quotes carrying the escapes `\"`, `\\`, `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\0` and `\uXXXX` with exactly four hexadecimal digits; a literal string in single quotes carrying no escapes; an array of values in `[` and `]`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing one trailing comma; or an inline table of `<dotted name> = <value>` pairs in `{` and `}`, separated by commas, possibly empty and allowing no trailing comma. Arrays and inline tables may hold each other. A bare word that is none of these is an error naming that word, while a value required but never written, because the line ends or a `,`, a `]` or a `}` comes first, is `expected a value`. Anything but spaces, tabs and a comment after the value is an error.

`json` prints the document as JSON indented by two spaces, with the members of every object in ascending key order by code point, and a trailing newline; an array of tables prints as a JSON array, and a float prints however JSON prints its number, so a float that happens to be whole prints without a fraction. `keys` instead prints one line per node below the root, `<path> <type>`, walking objects in ascending key order and arrays in index order, depth first, each node before its children. A path joins object keys with `.` and appends `[i]` for an array index, using the key text as written after decoding. The type is `table`, `array`, `string`, `integer`, `float` or `boolean`, and an array of tables is an `array`.

src: block.js cli.js html.js inline.js refs.js test: mdlite.test.js spec.test.js ---README--- # mdlite A small Markdown-to-HTML converter with no dependencies. It reads a document from standard input and writes HTML, or the document's outline, to standard output. ## Layout | File | What it owns | | --- | --- | | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported | | `src/block.js` | the block grammar — fences, headings, lists, paragraphs — and the rendering of each | | `src/inline.js` | the inline grammar: escapes, code spans, emphasis, and links | | `src/html.js` | `escapeText` and `escapeAttribute` | `test/mdlite.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the link-definition files the examples name. ## Blocks The document is split on newlines and the empty tail a trailing newline leaves is dropped. A line is then read as one of these, in this order. A line of three or more backticks with no further backtick on it opens a fenced code block, and its info string is the rest of the line, trimmed, of which the first word is used. The fence closes at the first later line that is nothing but backticks, at least as many as the opening had, and everything between the two is content. A fence that never closes fails. A blank line ends whatever block was open. `#` to `######` followed by a space is a heading of that level, over the trimmed rest of the line. `- ` at the very start of a line is a bullet item, unless a paragraph is already open, in which case it is one of that paragraph's lines. Anything else is a paragraph line, trimmed. Each block renders to `

` to `

`, `

` with its lines joined by newlines, `

    ` with one `
  • ` per item on its own line, or `
    ` with the content copied in, `class="language-"` when there is an info string. The blocks are joined with newlines and the output ends with one; an empty document renders nothing at all.

## Inline

A backslash before one of `` \ ` * [ ] ( ) `` writes that character literally. A backtick pair is a code span, with its content escaped. `**` pairs make `` and `*` pairs make ``, each rendering its content inline. `[text](url)` is a link, with the text rendered inline and the url escaped for the attribute. An unmatched marker is literal text. Everything else is escaped for HTML.

## Modes

- `html` writes the rendered document.
- `outline` writes one line per heading, ` `.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. An unterminated fence is `error: line N: unterminated code fence`, naming the line the fence opened on. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.

## Known gaps

A list is flat: an indented `- ` is a paragraph line, not a nested item. There are no reference links, so `[text][label]` is literal text and a `[label]: url` line renders as a paragraph. Fence content is copied out verbatim, so a `<` in a code block escapes into the surrounding HTML and a document that shows HTML in a code block renders wrong.

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.

This task is a completion exercise: every file and function in this workspace already holds its final implementation except `digestBytes` in `src/digest.js`, whose body currently throws 'not implemented'. Implement only that function's body so it fulfills the specification above; keep its signature exactly as given, and do not edit any other file, export, or function. 1: # taskrun
2: 
3: A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
11: | `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
12: | `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |
13: 
14: `test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
15: 
16: ## The task file
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.
19: 
20: ```
21: # build.tasks
22: task build node build.js
23: task bundle node bundle.js
24: needs bundle build
25: ```
26: 
27: `task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
28: 
29: ## Modes
30: 
31: - `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
32: - `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
33: - `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.
34: 
35: ## Failures
36: 
37: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.
38: 
39: ## Known gaps
40: 
41: `order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

(End of file - total 41 lines)

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `order`, `show <name>`, `files <name>`, `digest <path>...` and `plan <snapshot>`. */
3: 
4: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { digestBytes } from './digest.js'
6: import { CycleError, order } from './graph.js'
7: import { parse, ParseError, splitLines } from './parse.js'
8: import { plan, readSnapshot, SnapshotError } from './plan.js'
9: 
10: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>'
11: 
12: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
13: function fail(message, code = 2) {
14:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
15:   process.exit(code)
16: }
17: 
18: /** One `files` field, with `-` standing for an empty list. */
19: function field(label, values) {
20:   return `${label}: ${values.length === 0 ? '-' : [...values].sort().join(' ')}`
21: }
22: 
23: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
24: const mode = argv[0]
25: const arity = { order: 1, show: 2, files: 2, plan: 2 }
26: if (mode === 'digest' ? argv.length < 2 : argv.length !== arity[mode]) fail(USAGE)
27: 
28: let tasks
29: try {
30:   tasks = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')))

1: /** The task-file parser: directives to tasks, with the failures the specification words. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const PATH = /^[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line it was read from, or 0 when it names none. */
7: export class ParseError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'ParseError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /** Whether a word is a usable task name. */
20: function isName(word) {
21:   return NAME.test(word)
22: }
23: 
24: /** Whether a word is a usable workspace path. */
25: function isPath(word) {
26:   return PATH.test(word) && !word.startsWith('/') && !word.split('/').includes('..')
27: }
28: 
29: /**
30:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
31:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
32:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
33:  */
34: export function splitLines(text) {
35:   const split = text.split('\n')
36:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
37:   return split
38: }
39: 
40: /** The field a directive attaches to, and the word the usage line names. */
41: const ATTACHING = new Map([
42:   ['needs', { field: 'needs', word: 'dependency' }],
43:   ['reads', { field: 'reads', word: 'path' }],
44:   ['writes', { field: 'writes', word: 'path' }],
45: ])
46: 
47: /**
48:  * Parse a task file into its tasks.
49:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
50:  * @returns {Map<string, {name: string, command: string, needs: string[], reads: string[], writes: string[]}>} the tasks by name, in declaration order.
51:  */
52: export function parse(lines) {
53:   const tasks = new Map()
54:   const referenced = []
55:   const attachments = []
56:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
57:     const line = index + 1
58:     const text = raw.trim()
59:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
60:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
61:     const attaching = ATTACHING.get(words[0])
62:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
63:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, 'expected task <name> <word>...')
64:       const name = words[1]
65:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
66:       if (tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `task ${name} is declared twice`)
67:       tasks.set(name, { name, command: words.slice(2).join(' '), needs: [], reads: [], writes: [] })
68:     } else if (attaching !== undefined) {
69:       if (words.length < 3) throw new ParseError(line, `expected ${words[0]} <name> <${attaching.word}>...`)
70:       const [, name, ...values] = words
71:       if (!isName(name)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${name}`)
72:       referenced.push(name)
73:       for (const value of values) {
74:         if (attaching.field === 'needs') {
75:           if (!isName(value)) throw new ParseError(line, `invalid task name ${value}`)
76:           referenced.push(value)
77:         } else if (!isPath(value)) {
78:           throw new ParseError(line, `invalid path ${value}`)
79:         }
80:       }
81:       attachments.push({ name, field: attaching.field, values })
82:     } else {
83:       throw new ParseError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
84:     }
85:   }
86:   for (const name of referenced) {
87:     if (!tasks.has(name)) throw new ParseError(0, `unknown task ${name}`)
88:   }
89:   for (const { name, field, values } of attachments) {
90:     const list = tasks.get(name)[field]
91:     for (const value of values) {
92:       if (!list.includes(value)) list.push(value)
93:     }
94:   }
95:   return tasks
96: }

1: /** Ordering the task graph, and naming the cycle that stops it. */
2: 
3: /** A dependency cycle, carrying the names that close it. */
4: export class CycleError extends Error {
5:   /**
6:    * @param {string[]} names - the cycle from the re-entered task back to itself, the repeat included.
7:    */
8:   constructor(names) {
9:     super(`cycle: ${names.join(' -> ')}`)
10:     this.name = 'CycleError'
11:     this.names = names
12:   }
13: }
14: 
15: /**
16:  * The cycle a depth-first search finds first, or undefined when the graph is acyclic.
17:  * The search starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's
18:  * dependencies in ascending name order; the cycle runs from the task the search
19:  * re-entered, through the stack, back to that task.
20:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
21:  * @returns {string[] | undefined} the cycle's names, the repeat included.
22:  */
23: export function findCycle(tasks) {
24:   const names = [...tasks.keys()].sort()
25:   const done = new Set()
26:   const stack = []
27:   const onStack = new Set()
28:   const walk = (name) => {
29:     if (onStack.has(name)) return [...stack.slice(stack.indexOf(name)), name]
30:     if (done.has(name)) return undefined
31:     stack.push(name)
32:     onStack.add(name)
33:     for (const need of [...tasks.get(name).needs].sort()) {
34:       const found = walk(need)
35:       if (found !== undefined) return found
36:     }
37:     stack.pop()
38:     onStack.delete(name)
39:     done.add(name)
40:     return undefined
41:   }
42:   for (const name of names) {
43:     const found = walk(name)
44:     if (found !== undefined) return found
45:   }
46:   return undefined
47: }
48: 
49: /**
50:  * The tasks in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose
51:  * dependencies have all been emitted.
52:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
53:  * @returns {string[]} the names in run order.
54:  * @throws {CycleError} when a dependency cycle leaves the order undefined.
55:  */
56: export function order(tasks) {
57:   const cycle = findCycle(tasks)
58:   if (cycle !== undefined) throw new CycleError(cycle)
59:   const remaining = new Set(tasks.keys())
60:   const emitted = new Set()
61:   const out = []
62:   while (remaining.size > 0) {
63:     const ready = [...remaining].filter(name => tasks.get(name).needs.every(need => emitted.has(need))).sort()
64:     const next = ready[0]
65:     remaining.delete(next)
66:     emitted.add(next)
67:     out.push(next)
68:   }
69:   return out
70: }

1: /** The snapshot reader and the staleness rule that decides what a plan runs. */
2: 
3: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
4: import { digestBytes } from './digest.js'
5: import { order } from './graph.js'
6: 
7: const DIGEST = /^[0-9a-f]{8}$/
8: 
9: /** One refusal of a snapshot file, carrying the file and the 1-based line. */
10: export class SnapshotError extends Error {
11:   /**
12:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the `error: ` prefix.
13:    */
14:   constructor(message) {
15:     super(message)
16:     this.name = 'SnapshotError'
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /**
21:  * Read one snapshot file into the digests it records.
22:  * @param {string} path - the snapshot's workspace path, as the argument gave it.
23:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} the recorded digest of each path.
24:  * @throws {SnapshotError} when the file is unreadable or a line is malformed.
25:  */
26: export function readSnapshot(path) {
27:   if (!existsSync(path)) throw new SnapshotError(`cannot read snapshot ${path}`)
28:   const recorded = new Map()
29:   const lines = readFileSync(path, 'utf8').split('\n')
30:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
31:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
32:     const line = index + 1
33:     const text = raw.trim()
34:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
35:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
36:     if (words.length !== 2) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: expected <path> <digest>`)
37:     if (!DIGEST.test(words[1])) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: invalid digest ${words[1]}`)
38:     if (recorded.has(words[0])) throw new SnapshotError(`${path}: line ${line}: path ${words[0]} is recorded twice`)
39:     recorded.set(words[0], words[1])
40:   }
41:   return recorded
42: }
43: 
44: /**
45:  * Why one watched path makes its task stale, or undefined when it does not.
46:  * @param {string} path - the watched workspace path.
47:  * @param {Map<string, string>} recorded - the snapshot's digests.
48:  * @returns {string | undefined} the reason, as the plan line words it.
49:  */
50: function pathReason(path, recorded) {
51:   if (!recorded.has(path)) return `new ${path}`
52:   if (!existsSync(path)) return `missing ${path}`
53:   return digestBytes(readFileSync(path)) === recorded.get(path) ? undefined : `changed ${path}`
54: }
55: 
56: /**
57:  * Decide, for every task in run order, whether the plan runs it and why.
58:  * @param {Map<string, {needs: string[], reads: string[], writes: string[]}>} tasks - the parsed tasks.
59:  * @param {Map<string, string>} recorded - the snapshot's digests.
60:  * @returns {{name: string, reason: string | undefined}[]} one decision per task, in run order.
61:  */
62: export function plan(tasks, recorded) {
63:   const running = new Set()
64:   return order(tasks).map((name) => {
65:     const task = tasks.get(name)
66:     const watched = [...new Set([...task.reads, ...task.writes])].sort()
67:     let reason
68:     for (const path of watched) {
69:       reason = pathReason(path, recorded)
70:       if (reason !== undefined) break
71:     }
72:     if (reason === undefined) {
73:       const stale = [...task.needs].sort().find(need => running.has(need))
74:       if (stale !== undefined) reason = `needs ${stale}`
75:     }
76:     if (reason !== undefined) running.add(name)
77:     return { name, reason }
78:   })
79: }

## Solution Summary

I implemented the `digestBytes` function in `src/digest.js` that computes the **32-bit FNV-1a hash** of a byte buffer and returns it as an 8-character lowercase hexadecimal string.

### Implementation Details:

```javascript
export function digestBytes(bytes) {
  let hash = OFFSET
  for (let i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) {
    hash ^= bytes[i]
    hash = Math.imul(hash, PRIME)
  }
  return (hash >>> 0).toString(16).padStart(8, '0')
}
```

### Key Points:

1. **FNV-1a Algorithm**: 
   - Initialize hash with OFFSET (0x811c9dc5)
   - For each byte: XOR the hash with the byte, then multiply by PRIME (16777619)

2. **32-bit Multiplication**: Used `Math.imul()` for proper 32-bit integer multiplication instead of the regular `*` operator, which uses floating-point and can lose precision with large numbers

3. **Unsigned Conversion**: Used `>>> 0` to convert the signed 32-bit result to unsigned before converting to hex

4. **Hex Formatting**: Padded with leading zeros to ensure exactly 8 lowercase hexadecimal digits

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.

Implement only that function's body so it fulfills the specification above; keep its signature exactly as given, and do not edit any other file, export, or function. This is a visible-test tier: your certificate comes from the suite under test/, not from a held-back corpus.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `json` or `keys`, and reads a configuration document from standard input. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every directive fits on one line. Exit 0 whenever the document parses.

A line whose first character that is not a space or a tab is `#` or `;`, and a line holding only spaces and tabs, contributes nothing. Elsewhere a `#` or a `;` outside a quoted string ends the line, and what follows it is ignored; a `#` that a value runs into without whitespace before it is part of that value's text and makes it invalid.

A name is a bare word of one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_` and `-`, or a quoted string. A dotted name is names joined by `.`, with spaces and tabs allowed around each `.`.

A line beginning with `[` is a header. `[name]` makes that table current, creating the tables on the way; when the name already holds anything other than a table the reason is `<path> is not a table`, and otherwise a table a header already made current may not be named by a second `[name]` header, though a table that only came into being on the way to a deeper one, or from a dotted key, still may. `[[name]]` appends a fresh table to the array of tables at that name, creating it when it is absent, and makes that fresh table current; when the name already holds anything other than an array of tables the reason is `<path> is not an array of tables`. 24:  * @param lines - the input lines, in order.

32:   for (let index = 0; index < lines.length; index += 1) {

34:     try {

36:       reader.skip()
37:       const first = reader.peek()
38:       if (first === undefined || first === '#' || first === ';') continue
39:       if (first === '[') {

42:         const parts = reader.name()
43:         if (!reader.eat(']') || (array && !reader.eat(']'))) throw new ConfError('unterminated table header')
44:         endOfLine(reader, 'a table header')
45:         const parent = descend(root, parts.slice(0, -1), [])

47:         const held = parent.value.get(last)
48:         if (array) {

65:         continue

70:       const held = reader.value([...currentPath, ...parts].join('.'))

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. 1: # taskrun
2: 
3: A dependency-aware task runner with no dependencies of its own. It reads a task file from standard input and answers questions about it; it never executes a command.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the task-file grammar and the refusals it words, as `ParseError` |
11: | `src/graph.js` | run order over the dependency edges |
12: | `src/digest.js` | the FNV-1a digest the snapshot format records |
13: 
14: `test/taskrun.test.js` is the suite for what is already here. `data/files/` holds the workspace files the examples name, and `data/snapshots/` the digest snapshots.
15: 
16: ## The task file
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace.
19: 
20: ```
21: # build.tasks
22: task build node build.js
23: task bundle node bundle.js
24: needs bundle build
25: ```
26: 
27: `task <name> <word>...` declares a task whose command is the remaining words joined with single spaces. `needs <name> <dependency>...` adds dependencies; a repeated edge counts once, and a `needs` line may stand before the `task` line it names.
28: 
29: ## Modes
30: 
31: - `order` prints the task names one per line, in run order: repeatedly the lexicographically smallest task whose dependencies have all been printed.
32: - `show <name>` prints `<name>: <command>` and then `needs: ` followed by the dependencies in ascending order, or `-` when there are none.
33: - `digest <path>...` prints `<path> <digest>` for each path in argument order, with `missing` in place of a digest for a path that is not there. The digest is 32-bit FNV-1a over the file's bytes — offset basis `0x811c9dc5`, prime `16777619`, xor then multiply — as eight lowercase hex digits.
34: 
35: ## Failures
36: 
37: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A parse failure names its 1-based input line: `error: line 2: unknown directive run`. The messages are `expected task <name> <word>...`, `expected needs <name> <dependency>...`, `invalid task name <name>`, `task <name> is declared twice` and `unknown directive <word>`. A `needs` line naming a task no `task` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown task <name>`, and so is `show` on such a name.
38: 
39: ## Known gaps
40: 
41: `order` does not detect a dependency cycle: it stops as soon as nothing is ready and leaves every task in the cycle out of its output. The task file has no way to declare which files a task reads or writes, so nothing here can tell whether a task is up to date.

`taskrun` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/taskrun.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Extend it so the task file can declare the files a task touches, so a dependency cycle is reported instead of silently truncating the order, and so a plan can say which tasks a snapshot leaves stale. Every behaviour `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is, including the wording and the exit code of every failure it lists, and the work spans the parser, the graph, and the command.

Two directives join the task file, parsed like the ones already there. `reads <name> <path>...` names input files of a task and `writes <name> <path>...` names its outputs; each takes at least one path, a repeated path counts once, and either line may stand before the `task` line it names, exactly as `needs` may. A path is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.`, `/` and `-`, does not begin with `/`, and holds no `..` segment; anything else fails with `error: line N: invalid path <path>`. A `reads` or `writes` line with fewer than two words after the directive fails with `error: line N: expected reads <name> <path>...` or `error: line N: expected writes <name> <path>...`. Every name a `reads` or `writes` line uses must be declared by a `task` line somewhere, on pain of the existing line-less `error: unknown task <name>`; as before, every failure that names a line is reported before that one, in line order.

`files <name>` is a new mode taking exactly one name. It prints `reads: ` followed by that task's input paths in ascending order and then `writes: ` followed by its output paths in ascending order, each with `-` in place of an empty list, and it refuses an undeclared name the way `show` does. The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js order|show <name>|files <name>|digest <path>...|plan <snapshot>`; `order` takes no further word, `show`, `files` and `plan` take exactly one, and `digest` takes at least one.

`order` now refuses a cyclic graph: it writes `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exits 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task. A task that needs itself is such a cycle. `show`, `files` and `digest` never look at the graph, so they answer a cyclic file as they answer any other.

`plan <snapshot>` reads a digest snapshot and reports what the graph would have to rerun. The snapshot file is a line per recorded path, trimmed, with an empty line and a line starting with `#` ignored, and the rest split on runs of whitespace into exactly two words: a path and its digest, which is exactly eight lowercase hexadecimal digits. A snapshot that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read snapshot <path>`, and a malformed line fails with `error: <snapshot>: line N: ` followed by `expected <path> <digest>`, `invalid digest <word>`, or `path <path> is recorded twice`, where N counts the snapshot's own lines from 1. The snapshot is read after the task file is parsed and before the graph is walked, so a task-file failure precedes a snapshot failure, and a snapshot failure precedes a cycle.

A task's watched paths are its inputs and its outputs together, deduplicated and taken in ascending order. The first watched path with a reason decides that the task runs, and the reason is `new <path>` when the snapshot records no digest for it, `missing <path>` when the snapshot records one but the workspace has no such file, and `changed <path>` when the file's digest differs from the recorded one; a file whose digest matches gives no reason. A task no watched path condemns runs anyway when some dependency runs, with the reason `needs <dep>` naming the lexicographically smallest dependency that runs, so a path reason always wins over a dependency one. `plan` prints one line per task in the order `order` prints, `run <name> <reason>` or `skip <name>`, and then a final line `total run=<r> skip=<s>` counting the two.

`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares.

31:  * List scheduling onto a fixed number of workers: at every instant a free
32:  * worker takes the ready task with the longest remaining chain, ties broken by
33:  * name, and a task of cost 0 frees its worker at the instant it starts.
34:  * @param tasks - an acyclic graph.
35:  * @param workers - how many workers run in parallel, at least 1.
36:  * @returns per worker the tasks it ran with their start and finish, and the makespan.
37:  */
38: export function pack(tasks, workers) {
39:   const priority = chains(tasks)
40:   const assigned = new Map()
41:   const lanes = Array.from({ length: workers }, () => [])
42:   const free = Array.from({ length: workers }, () => 0)
43:   const pending = new Set(tasks.keys())
44:   let now = 0
45:   while (pending.size > 0) {
46:     // Readiness is recomputed after every placement, because a task of cost 0
47:     // finishes at the instant it starts and can unblock its dependents at once.
48:     for (;;) {
49:       const worker = free.findIndex(when => when <= now)
50:       if (worker === -1) break
51:       const ready = [...pending]
52:         .filter(name => tasks.get(name).deps.every(dependency => (assigned.get(dependency)?.finish ?? Infinity) <= now))
53:         .sort((left, right) => priority.get(right) - priority.get(left) || (left < right ? -1 : 1))
54:       if (ready.length === 0) break
55:       const name = ready[0]
56:       const finish = now + tasks.get(name).cost
57:       assigned.set(name, { worker, start: now, finish })
58:       lanes[worker].push({ name, start: now, finish })
59:       free[worker] = finish
60:       pending.delete(name)
61:     }
62:     if (pending.size === 0) break
63:     // Nothing more fits at this instant, so advance to the next moment a worker
64:     // frees up; an acyclic graph always leaves one such moment ahead.

## Implementation Summary

I successfully implemented the `findCycle` function in `src/graph.js`. The function detects cycles in a directed graph using a depth-first search algorithm.

### Algorithm Details:

1. **State Tracking**: Uses a `Map` to track three states for each task:
   - `undefined` (unvisited)
   - `'visiting'` (currently in the DFS path)
   - `'visited'` (completely processed)

2. **DFS Path**: Maintains a `stack` array to track the current path during traversal.

3. **Cycle Detection**: When visiting a task:
   - If already `'visited'`, skip it (already processed)
   - If currently `'visiting'`, a cycle is found - reconstruct it from the re-entered task through the stack back to itself
   - Otherwise, mark as `'visiting'`, process all dependencies recursively, then mark as `'visited'`

4. **Search Order**: Starts DFS from each task in ascending name order, walking each task's dependencies in ascending name order (which are already sorted in the parsed graph).

5. **Return Value**: 
   - Returns an array like `['a', 'b', 'a']` representing the cycle from the first repeated task back to itself
   - Returns `undefined` if no cycle exists

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. 1: /** The build graph: parsing the directive lines, and the cycle report a bad graph earns. */
2: 
3: /** Raised for input the specification rejects; `line` is 0 when the failure has no line. */
4: export class GraphError extends Error {
5:   /**
6:    * @param message - the reported reason.
7:    * @param line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names none.
8:    */
9:   constructor(message, line) {
10:     super(message)
11:     this.name = 'GraphError'
12:     this.line = line
13:   }
14: }
15: 
16: /** A task name: letters, digits, underscore, dash and dot, at least one character. */
17: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/u
18: 
19: /** A cost: an unsigned decimal integer with no sign and no separators. */
20: const COST = /^\d+$/u
21: 
22: /**
23:  * Parse the directive lines into tasks and their dependency sets.
24:  * @param lines - the input lines, in order.
25:  * @returns a map from task name to `{ cost, deps }`, with `deps` a sorted array of names.
26:  * @throws {GraphError} for an unknown directive, a bad cost, a redeclared task, or a name never declared.
27:  */
28: export function parse(lines) {
29:   const tasks = new Map()
30:   const edges = []
31:   for (let index = 0; index < lines.length; index += 1) {
32:     const line = lines[index].trim()
33:     const at = index + 1
34:     if (line === '' || line.startsWith('#')) continue
35:     const words = line.split(/\s+/u)
36:     if (words[0] === 'task') {
37:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new GraphError('expected task <name> <cost>', at)
38:       if (!NAME.test(words[1])) throw new GraphError(`invalid task name ${words[1]}`, at)
39:       if (!COST.test(words[2])) throw new GraphError('cost must be a non-negative integer', at)
40:       if (tasks.has(words[1])) throw new GraphError(`task ${words[1]} is declared twice`, at)
41:       tasks.set(words[1], { cost: Number(words[2]), deps: new Set() })
42:       continue
43:     }
44:     if (words[0] === 'dep') {
45:       if (words.length < 3) throw new GraphError('expected dep <name> <dependency>...', at)
46:       for (const word of words.slice(1)) {
47:         if (!NAME.test(word)) throw new GraphError(`invalid task name ${word}`, at)
48:       }
49:       for (const dependency of words.slice(2)) edges.push([words[1], dependency])
50:       continue
51:     }
52:     throw new GraphError(`unknown directive ${words[0]}`, at)
53:   }
54:   for (const [name, dependency] of edges) {
55:     for (const referenced of [name, dependency]) {
56:       if (!tasks.has(referenced)) throw new GraphError(`unknown task ${referenced}`, 0)
57:     }
58:     tasks.get(name).deps.add(dependency)
59:   }
60:   return new Map([...tasks.entries()]
61:     .map(([name, task]) => [name, { cost: task.cost, deps: [...task.deps].sort() }]))
62: }
63: 
64: /**
65:  * The first cycle a name-ordered depth-first search meets, walking each task's
66:  * dependencies in name order.
67:  * @param tasks - the parsed graph.
68:  * @returns the cycle as names from the repeated task back to itself, or `undefined` when the graph is acyclic.
69:  */
70: export function findCycle(tasks) {
71:   throw new Error('not implemented')
72: }
73: 
74: /**
75:  * Earliest finish time of every task with unlimited workers, which is also the
76:  * cost of the longest chain ending at it.
77:  * @param tasks - an acyclic graph.
78:  * @returns a map from name to `{ start, finish, depth }`.
79:  */
80: export function timings(tasks) {
81:   const out = new Map()
82:   const visit = name => {
83:     const known = out.get(name)
84:     if (known !== undefined) return known
85:     const task = tasks.get(name)
86:     let start = 0
87:     let depth = 0
88:     for (const dependency of task.deps) {
89:       const resolved = visit(dependency)
90:       start = Math.max(start, resolved.finish)
91:       depth = Math.max(depth, resolved.depth + 1)
92:     }
93:     const timing = { start, finish: start + task.cost, depth }
94:     out.set(name, timing)
95:     return timing
96:   }
97:   for (const name of [...tasks.keys()].sort()) visit(name)
98:   return out
99: }
100: 
101: /**
102:  * The cost of the longest chain that starts at each task, used as the priority
103:  * of the packing scheduler.
104:  * @param tasks - an acyclic graph.
105:  * @returns a map from name to that chain's total cost, including the task itself.
106:  */
107: export function chains(tasks) {
108:   const dependents = new Map([...tasks.keys()].map(name => [name, []]))
109:   for (const [name, task] of tasks) {
110:     for (const dependency of task.deps) dependents.get(dependency).push(name)
111:   }
112:   const out = new Map()
113:   const visit = name => {
114:     const known = out.get(name)
115:     if (known !== undefined) return known
116:     let longest = 0
117:     for (const dependent of dependents.get(name).sort()) longest = Math.max(longest, visit(dependent))
118:     const total = tasks.get(name).cost + longest
119:     out.set(name, total)
120:     return total
121:   }
122:   for (const name of [...tasks.keys()].sort()) visit(name)
123:   return out
124: }

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It reads a build graph from standard input and takes one of three argument forms: `waves`, `explain`, or `pack` followed by a worker count. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves. Trim each line; ignore it when it is empty or begins with `#`; otherwise split it on runs of whitespace.

A `task <name> <cost>` line declares a task. A name is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. A cost is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign and without separators, so `01` is the cost 1. A `dep <name> <dependency>...` line makes the first name depend on every later name on the line; a repeated edge counts once, and a `dep` line may appear before the tasks it names. Every name a `dep` line uses must be declared by some `task` line somewhere in the input. An empty input is a valid graph with no task.

`waves` prints one line per wave, `wave K: ` followed by the wave's task names in ascending order separated by single spaces, and then a final line `total T`. Wave 0 holds every task with no dependency and wave K holds every task whose deepest dependency is in wave K-1. `T` is the makespan with unlimited workers: the greatest finish time, or 0 when there is no task. A task's start is the greatest finish of its dependencies, or 0 when it has none, and its finish is its start plus its cost.

`explain` prints one line per task in ascending name order, `<name> start=<s> finish=<f> depth=<d>`, where the start and finish are the ones above and the depth is the wave the task sits in, and then the same final `total T` line.

`pack <workers>` simulates the same graph on that many workers. Time starts at 0. While a worker is free at the current instant and some task is ready, meaning every one of its dependencies has already finished at or before that instant, take the ready task with the greatest priority, breaking ties by ascending name, and start it on the free worker with the smallest index. A task's priority is the cost of the longest chain that begins at it, counting its own cost and then the costs down to any task that nothing depends on. A task of cost 0 finishes at the instant it starts, so its worker is free again at once and its dependents may start in the same instant. When nothing more can start, time advances to the next instant at which a worker becomes free, and the loop repeats. The output is one line per worker in index order, `worker <i>:` followed by ` <name>@<start>-<finish>` for each task it ran in the order it ran them, and then a final line `makespan M` holding the greatest finish, or 0 when there is no task.

A cycle makes the graph unschedulable: write `error: cycle: ` followed by the cycle's names joined with ` -> ` and ending with a repeat of the first name, then exit 3, having written nothing to standard output. The reported cycle is the first one a depth-first search finds when it starts from each task in ascending name order and walks each task's dependencies in ascending name order; it runs from the task the search re-entered, through the search stack, back to that task.

Every other failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js waves|explain|pack <workers>` when the arguments are not one of the three forms; `error: workers must be a positive integer` when the worker count is not a decimal integer of at least 1 written without a sign or a leading zero; `error: line N: expected task <name> <cost>` and `error: line N: expected dep <name> <dependency>...` when a directive has the wrong number of words; `error: line N: invalid task name <name>` for a name outside the allowed characters; `error: line N: cost must be a non-negative integer`; `error: line N: task <name> is declared twice`; `error: line N: unknown directive <word>`; and `error: unknown task <name>`, with no line number, for the first name in input order that a `dep` line uses and no `task` line declares.

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: /** The command: `html`, `outline` and `defs`, each over the document on standard input. */
3: 
4: import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
5: import { BlockError, headings, parse, render, splitLines } from './block.js'
6: import { define, readDefinition, RefError } from './refs.js'
7: 
8: const USAGE = 'usage: cli.js html|outline|defs [<definitions>]'
9: 
10: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
11: function fail(message) {
12:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
13:   process.exit(2)
14: }
15: 
16: /** The definitions one file carries, refused at its own line when a line is not a definition. */
17: function fileDefinitions(path) {
18:   if (!existsSync(path)) fail(`cannot read definitions ${path}`)
19:   const table = new Map()
20:   for (const [index, raw] of splitLines(readFileSync(path, 'utf8')).entries()) {
21:     const line = index + 1
22:     if (raw.trim() === '' || raw.trim().startsWith('#')) continue
23:     const definition = readDefinition(raw)
24:     if (definition === undefined) fail(`${path}: line ${line}: expected [label]: <url>`)
25:     try {
26:       define(table, line, definition, 'file')
27:     } catch (error) {
28:       if (!(error instanceof RefError)) throw error
29:       fail(`${path}: line ${line}: ${error.message}`)
30:     }
31:   }
32:   return table
33: }
34: 
35: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
36: const mode = argv[0]
37: if (!['html', 'outline', 'defs'].includes(mode) || argv.length > 2) fail(USAGE)
38: 
39: const definitions = argv.length === 2 ? fileDefinitions(argv[1]) : new Map()
40: 
41: let parsed
42: try {
43:   parsed = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')), definitions)
44: } catch (error) {
45:   if (!(error instanceof BlockError) && !(error instanceof RefError)) throw error
46:   fail(`line ${error.line}: ${error.message}`)
47: }
48: 
49: if (mode === 'html') {
50:   process.stdout.write(render(parsed, definitions))
51: } else if (mode === 'outline') {
52:   process.stdout.write(headings(parsed).map(one => `${one.level} ${one.text}\n`).join(''))
53: } else {
54:   const out = [...definitions].sort((left, right) => (left[0] < right[0] ? -1 : 1))
55:   process.stdout.write(`${out.map(([label, { url, source }]) => `${label} ${url} ${source}\n`).join('')}total ${out.length}\n`)
56: }
